summary: RFC 4379 defines MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute, where the Router Alert Option must be set in the IP header of the Echo Request messages. This document explains how IPv6 Router Alert Option is used for these messages. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some test messages have to carry a flag that asks routers along the path to examine them closely. The flag had a number for IPv4 but none for IPv6, so this document adds one number for IPv6 and updates the rulebook that says when to use it.

subtitle: Allocates IPv6 Router Alert value 69 so MPLS ping and traceroute messages are flagged for IPv6 routers.

tldr.problem: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute require the Router Alert Option in the IP header, but IPv4 has a generic option value for it and IPv6 had none that MPLS operations tools could use.
tldr.mechanism: The document allocates a new IPv6 Router Alert Option value, 69, for MPLS operations, administration and maintenance, and updates RFC 4379 so that value 69 MUST be used in IPv6 headers and the generic IPv4 value 0x0 SHOULD be used in IPv4 headers.
tldr.outcome: IANA assigned one new code point, 69 with the description MPLS OAM, in the IPv6 Router Alert Option Values registry. The document is now marked Historic, and it updated RFC 4379.

today: RFC 7506 is marked Historic. It was published in April 2015, it updated RFC 4379 and it has not been obsoleted by another RFC.

sections.title: Why MPLS OAM Needed an IPv6 Router Alert Value
sections.content:
A commonly deployed MPLS operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) tool is MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute, specified in RFC 4379, which is used to diagnose MPLS network data planes. It requires the Router Alert Option (RAO) in the IP header: Section 4.3 of that RFC states that the IP RAO MUST be set in the IP header of an MPLS Echo Request message, and Section 4.5 states the same for an MPLS Echo Reply when the Reply Mode in the Echo Request is set to Reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet with Router Alert.

For IPv4, RFC 2113 defines a generic Option Value of 0x0, assigned to Router shall examine packet, and that value is used in LSP Ping and LSP Traceroute for MPLS in IPv4 environments. For IPv6, RFC 2711 defined the Router Alert for a general IPv6 purpose but required the Value field in the RAO to indicate a specific reason for using it. Because no value was defined for MPLS LSP Ping/Traceroute use or for general use, it was not possible for MPLS OAM tools to use the IPv6 Router Alert mechanism.

As vendors started to implement MPLS on the IPv6 control plane, a value was needed in order to comply with RFC 4379. The document also closes the gap discussed in the third paragraph of Section 3.4.2 of RFC 7439.
sections.plainLanguage: Some test messages have to carry a flag that asks routers along the path to examine them closely. The flag had a number for IPv4 but none for IPv6, so the test tools could not follow the rules on IPv6 networks.

sections.title: The New IPv6 Router Alert Option Value
sections.content:
The document defines a new Option Value, 69, for the IPv6 Router Alert Option. It alerts transit routers to examine the packet more closely for MPLS OAM purposes, and any MPLS OAM application that requires its packets to be examined by a transit router can use it.

Within this document, the value is used by the MPLS Echo Request and the MPLS Echo Reply for their IPv6 messages, as RFC 4379 requires. The abstract adds that the value applies to all MPLS OAM and is not limited to LSP Ping/Traceroute.
sections.plainLanguage: Number 69 is the new flag for IPv6. Any operations tool for these networks can add it when it wants the routers along the path to take a closer look at the packet.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 4379
sections.content:
Sections 4.3 and 4.5 of RFC 4379 are updated. Every time the Router Alert IP Option is mentioned there, the following text is appended.

The appended text makes the IPv4 behavior a recommendation and the IPv6 behavior a firm requirement: the generic IPv4 RAO value 0x0 SHOULD be used in an IPv4 header, and the IPv6 RAO value 69 MUST be used in an IPv6 header.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook now gets one extra sentence: use the old flag number on IPv4, and use flag 69 on IPv6.

sections.title: The IANA Registry Entry
sections.content: IANA has assigned a new code point under its IPv6 Router Alert Option Values registry, which RFC 2711 defined and RFC 5350 updated. The new entry is value 69, with the description MPLS OAM and a reference to RFC 7506.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of flag numbers got one new line, saying that 69 means MPLS test messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security concerns in addition to what has already been captured in RFC 4379 and RFC 6398, the latter of which expands the security considerations of RFC 2113 and RFC 2711.

IPv6 packets containing the MPLS OAM RAO are encapsulated with an MPLS header and are not expected to be inspected by every label switched hop within an MPLS LSP. The value of the RAO will therefore be processed by the appropriate router and is not subject to the problem of being ignored, as described in Section 2.2 of RFC 7045.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding this flag opens no new hole. The packets travel inside an MPLS header, so they are not read by every hop in the path, only by the router that is meant to act on them.

viz.caption: RAO VALUE TO USE IN MPLS ECHO MESSAGES

data.title: Router Alert IP Option, appended text
data.code:
In case of an IPv4 header, the generic IPv4 RAO value 0x0
[RFC2113] SHOULD be used.  In case of an IPv6 header, the IPv6 RAO
value (69) allocated through this document for MPLS OAM MUST be
used.
